title: The Late Confession
premise: Ada Zhou, coroner of the fading town of Marrow Creek, receives a confession letter for a drowning ruled accidental seven years ago—postmarked one day after the victim's mother was buried, and signed by a witness everyone insists died in that same incident. As the statute of limitations ticks down, Ada's quiet filing system of town secrets becomes both her map and her target, forcing her to choose between protecting the powerful families who keep the town alive and honoring the dead woman she once autopsied. The trail leads to a reclusive river keeper presumed dead but living under another name, whose testimony can reopen the case only if he survives to give it. In the end, Ada chooses justice outside the law: she publishes the truth herself, burns her own careful archive, and leaves town with the witness, trading invisibility for exile.
about_author: Rafael Sterling is the pen name of a former rural paramedic who spent a decade answering calls in towns too small for their own police force. He writes mysteries about institutions that outlast the people they were meant to protect.

chapters.title: Alphabetical by Surname
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. We meet her methodical world: the morgue, the ledgers, the graves she knows like neighbors. She files the last paperwork on Eleanor Voss's funeral and goes home to an empty house. Emotional beat: the comfort and loneliness of order.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A letter arrives confessing to the drowning death of Daniel Voss seven years prior, postmarked the day after his mother's funeral, unsigned except for a single initial: R. Ada recognizes handwriting quirks from old county records. Emotional beat: dread dressed as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Drowning File
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, with flashbacks. She pulls her own autopsy report and finds the anomalies she once filed away rather than questioned—bruising inconsistent with water entry. Sheriff Dale Pruitt, her old ally, warns her off. Emotional beat: complicity surfacing.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears He's Dead
chapters.summary: Ada interviews townsfolk about Raymond 'Ray' Okafor, the witness named obliquely in the letter, officially drowned alongside Daniel. Each account is polished, rehearsed, identical. Emotional beat: the uncanny unanimity of a lying town.

chapters.title: What Eleanor Knew
chapters.summary: Eleanor Voss's POV via letters found among her effects. For years she wrote to an unnamed recipient demanding the truth; the replies stopped three years ago. Ada realizes the confession may have been triggered by Eleanor's death—or her final letter. Emotional beat: grief as investigation.

chapters.title: The Statute Clock
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A retired judge confirms the window to reopen the case closes in six weeks. Pruitt begins quietly obstructing her records requests. First sign someone is watching her office at night. Emotional beat: time turning from resource to threat.

chapters.title: Bruises and Bookkeeping
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Cross-referencing old supply orders, she finds the marina dock repaired the week after the drowning—paid by the Hollis family, whose son Marcus dated Daniel's sister. Emotional beat: money revealing motive where memory won't.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Stayed
chapters.summary: June Voss's POV. Daniel's sister, who never believed the accident ruling, confronts Ada after finding her mother's correspondence missing. Instead of anger, she offers alliance—and a photograph of Ray taken two years after his supposed death. Emotional beat: reluctant trust.

chapters.title: River Keeper
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Following fuel purchases and fishing licenses, she narrows Ray's likely hiding place to a decommissioned lockhouse upriver. Pruitt announces budget cuts that will shutter the county archive—destroying her paper trail. Emotional beat: the walls closing politely.

chapters.title: The Lockhouse
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She finds Ray Okafor alive, gaunt and watchful, keeping the river's old locks out of habit. He admits writing the confession but refuses to testify: the last man who helped him had an 'accident.' Emotional beat: fear more persuasive than guilt.

chapters.title: Seven Years Underwater
chapters.summary: Ray's POV. His account of the night: he saw Marcus Hollis strike Daniel on the dock and flee; the town's silence was purchased with his own staged death, arranged by men he still fears. Emotional beat: testimony as wound reopened.

chapters.title: A Favor Called In
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She approaches the retired judge again, who reveals he was pressured during the original inquest and owes Eleanor a debt. He agrees to help—but only if Ada secures sworn testimony before the statute expires. Emotional beat: allies costing more than enemies.

chapters.title: Tail Lights on Ferry Road
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Returning from the lockhouse, she's run off the road by an unmarked truck. Her brakes survive; her certainty doesn't. She realizes Pruitt isn't just obstructing—he's reporting to the Hollises. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns Early
chapters.summary: June's POV. A fire guts the county records annex, destroying the original inquest file. June saves one box—her mother's letters—by arriving minutes early to collect them. Emotional beat: loss confirming what was worth destroying.

chapters.title: Marcus Comes Home
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Marcus Hollis returns to town for a chamber-of-commerce gala, all charm and campaign buttons—he's running for state office. At the gala he thanks Ada publicly for her 'service,' a message and a warning in one. Emotional beat: power smiling with teeth.

chapters.title: Deposition at Dawn
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The judge arranges a secret deposition at the lockhouse; Ray agrees, terrified. Pruitt discovers the plan through Ada's phone records and tips off the Hollis family attorney. Emotional beat: hope racing the leak.

chapters.title: Interrupted
chapters.summary: Ray's POV. Mid-deposition, armed men arrive posing as health inspectors. Ray escapes through the lock gates he alone knows how to work; the judge is hospitalized; the recording survives hidden in Ada's morgue cold storage. Emotional beat: sacrifice buying seconds.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Standing in the cemetery at night, Ada realizes the town itself is the evidence—the pattern of payments, repairs, and silences she has filed for seven years. She decides the law will fail, so the record must not. Emotional beat: duty inverted.

chapters.title: The Confession Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Climax, Ada's POV. At Eleanor's grave, before gathered townsfolk and a hidden recorder, Ada reads the confession aloud and names Marcus Hollis. Pruitt moves to arrest her; half the town stands between them. Emotional beat: the invisible woman made unignorable.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. With the statute expiring, formal charges collapse under the burned records—but the recording spreads online, and a state investigator opens a fresh case untouchable by local hands. Marcus resigns his campaign. Emotional beat: imperfect justice, real nonetheless.

chapters.title: Resignation Letter
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She tenders her resignation, packs nothing but Eleanor's letters, and meets Ray at the ferry landing. Pruitt lets them go, himself implicated and relieved. Emotional beat: leaving as its own verdict.

chapters.title: Unfiled
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ray and Ada alternating. Months later, in a coastal town where no one knows their names, a newspaper clipping arrives: the state indictment of Marcus Hollis. Ada starts a new ledger with no alphabetical system at all. Emotional beat: peace found outside the archive.
